body_markdown:
If you’re struggling to find room for your luggage, it may be time to ask whether you need all of it. Think about the types of trips you actually take. Do you need three enormous checked bags when you usually travel with a carry-on? Are you[storing a suitcase](https://www.publicstorage.com/blog/storage-tips/how-to-store-suitcases-and-travel-gear.html) with a broken wheel because you might fix it someday?


## **Key Takeaways**


- Most people can get by with a carry-on suitcase, a larger checked bag, and a personal item, but your travel habits may call for more or less.


- Think about how often you travel, how long you’re usually gone, and what you need to pack before deciding what luggage to keep.


- If two suitcases do basically the same job, you may not need both.


- Don’t automatically get rid of luggage you rarely use. Specialty bags can come in handy for certain trips.


- Donate luggage that’s still in good condition, and look into repair or recycling options for damaged bags.


- Nest smaller suitcases inside larger ones to save storage space.


## How Much Luggage Do I Need?


Go through your collection and ask:


- Have I used this suitcase in the past few years?


- Is it still in good condition?


- Does it fit my current travel needs?


- Do I have another bag that does the same job?


- Is it worth the storage space it takes up?


You don’t need to get rid of luggage just because you don’t use it every year. Large suitcases, garment bags, and specialty travel bags can be useful for occasional trips. But if you have bags you no longer want or need, consider donating them if they’re still in good condition.


## What Types of Luggage Should You Keep?


For most people, a small collection of luggage can cover just about any trip. Here are the types of bags you may want to keep:


- **Carry-on suitcase** : Good for weekend trips, short vacations, and traveling without checking a bag.


- **Large checked suitcase** : Handy for longer trips, bulky clothing, and vacations where you need to pack more.


- **Backpack or personal item** : Useful for keeping your wallet, electronics, medications, snacks, and other essentials close during travel.


- **Duffel bag** : Great for road trips, overnight stays, gym visits, and trips where you don’t need a traditional suitcase.


- **Garment bag** : Worth keeping if you regularly travel with suits, dresses, or other clothing you don’t want to wrinkle.


- **Specialty luggage** : Bags designed for sports equipment, photography gear, or other hobbies may be worth the space if you use them.


You probably don’t need one of everything on this list. If you always take road trips, you may use a duffel bag far more often than a rolling suitcase. If you fly frequently, a good carry-on may be the only suitcase you need.


## How Many Suitcases Does One Person Need?


One or two suitcases may be plenty for someone who travels occasionally. A carry-on for short trips and a larger suitcase for longer vacations can cover most situations.


Frequent travelers may want more options, especially if they take different types of trips. Someone who regularly travels for work might keep a dedicated carry-on packed with travel essentials, while a family that takes long vacations may need several checked bags.


Don’t get too hung up on a specific number. The goal is to keep luggage that you actually use, not to meet some imaginary suitcase limit.


## Do You Need a Suitcase For Every Family Member?


Not necessarily. It depends on how your family travels and how much everyone needs to pack. Young kiddos may not need their own large suitcases if their clothing can fit into a parent’s bag. Older kids and teens may prefer their own luggage, especially if they travel for school, sports, or other activities.


If your family usually takes road trips, sharing larger suitcases may work just fine. If everyone flies with a carry-on, individual bags may make more sense. Before buying or keeping a suitcase for every person, think about how many bags your family can realistically carry through an airport, load into a car, or fit into a hotel room. More bags can mean more chaos.


## Get Rid of Duplicate Luggage


Having two suitcases that are almost exactly the same size isn’t necessarily a problem, but do you actually use both? Line up your luggage and compare the bags. Look at their size, weight, condition, and features. If you have several carry-ons, for example, you may find that you always reach for the same one.


Keep the suitcase that works best for you and consider donating the extras. Pay attention to features you actually use, like spinner wheels, exterior pockets, expandable compartments, and handles that are comfortable to pull.


Don’t keep an older suitcase just because you spent a lot of money on it. If you have a better one that you always use instead, the old one may just be taking up space.


When you’re counting your luggage, don’t just look at rolling suitcases. Backpacks, duffel bags, weekender bags, garment bags, and other travel bags take up space, too. You may discover that you have five backpacks that all do basically the same thing or a stack of promotional duffel bags you’ve never used.


Gather them all in one place and decide which ones you actually need. You may want to keep a backpack for everyday use, a larger one for travel, and a duffel bag for overnight trips. The rest may be duplicates you can live without.


## Luggage FAQs


### **How many suitcases should one person own?**


One or two suitcases may be enough for most occasional travelers. A carry-on for shorter trips and a larger checked suitcase for longer vacations can cover many travel needs. Frequent travelers or people with special packing requirements may need more.


### **Do you need both a carry-on and a checked suitcase?**


Not always. If you usually take short trips and pack light, a carry-on may be all you need. A checked suitcase can be useful for longer trips, bulky belongings, or vacations where you need to bring more clothing and equipment.


### **How much luggage does a family of four need?**


It depends on the ages of the family members, how long you’re traveling, and how you get to your destination. Some families prefer a suitcase for each person, while others share larger bags. Think about how much luggage you can comfortably carry and transport before deciding.


### **Should I keep old suitcases?**


Keep old suitcases if they’re in good condition and you still have a use for them. If you always choose a newer bag instead, or the old suitcase has damage you don’t plan to repair, consider donating, selling, or recycling it.


### **Is it worth keeping expensive luggage you don’t use?**


Only if you have a reason to keep it. An expensive suitcase that doesn’t fit your current travel habits may be more useful to someone else. Consider selling it if it’s still in good condition.


### **Can you donate used suitcases?**


Yes. Many donation centers accept clean, functional suitcases, although rules vary. Call ahead or check the organization’s website before dropping them off.


### **How can I store multiple suitcases without taking up too much room?**


Try nesting smaller suitcases inside larger ones. You can also store luggage under beds, on closet shelves, or in other dry storage areas. If you don’t have enough room at home, a storage unit may be another option.


### **How often should you replace luggage?**


There’s no set replacement schedule. Keep using a suitcase as long as it’s functional and meets your travel needs. Broken wheels, damaged zippers, cracked shells, and handles that no longer work are signs that it may be time for a repair or replacement.
